section.title: Use risk and trust to set review depth
section.deck: An Instagram engineering leader distinguishes core-system scrutiny from fast peripheral changes and explains the conditions behind accepting with required fixes.

blocks.question: How do you decide how deeply to review a code change?
answer: The guest allocates review effort according to risk. Live production code and the core architecture receive close examination. A gated, noncritical leaf component may receive only a high-level review, including a check for serious problems such as security risks, because the blast radius and cost of rewriting it are smaller.

His trust in a known teammate is part of the calculation. This is not a philosophy he applies automatically to a new colleague, nor one he claims all Meta engineers share. He separates correctness and architectural risk from forcing every implementation to match his personal style.
blocks.speaker: Guest

followups.question: Do colleagues push back on quick approvals?
answer: Yes. His team knows it can explicitly request a deep review in the description or test plan, or return an approved change to review. The author may know that a superficially small component has a subtle performance or design issue. That signal changes the reviewer’s time allocation even if the component is still peripheral.

blocks.title: Match review effort to the cost of a mistake
rows: Mistakes can affect many engineers and be costly to repair
Smaller blast radius and easier testing or replacement
The author may see a hidden issue the reviewer missed
Ask for another review before landing
The necessary trust is not yet established

blocks.question: Why ask how to accept a change instead of how to reject it?
answer: He wants to identify what truly prevents safe progress: major architectural problems and critical bugs. He is less interested in making another engineer write the code exactly as he would. Greater experience can make reviewers more comfortable with several valid approaches.

He takes conditional approval unusually far. If he spots a bug that would break production, he may leave a clear warning and approve while explicitly requiring the author to fix it first. He says trusted colleagues have not landed such a known defect in his experience. For someone new, or a fix he doubts they can make correctly, he asks to be contacted again before landing.

The title and opening excerpt can obscure that condition. He is not claiming that deliberately shipping a known production-breaking bug is acceptable; he is relying on the author to resolve it before shipping. His reported track record does not prove that this convention is safe in every workflow.
blocks.speaker: Guest

blocks.heading: Speed is adjusted through feedback
blocks.text: The guest applies a similar idea to rollouts: if a small release produces healthy metrics and little adverse feedback, he may expand more quickly, then pull back when negative signals appear. He and the host accept some risk as the cost of learning and progress, while agreeing that repeatedly breaking production means moving too fast. This is a judgment based on system risk and visible feedback, not a fixed rollout schedule.
